chunks: "Through-hole parts have leads that go through holes in the board and get soldered on the other side.
Surface-mount parts sit flat on pads and are soldered on the same side by reflow.
SMT wins on size and density, because parts are much smaller, can sit on both sides of the board, and don't need drilled holes under every pin.

It also wins on cost at volume because pick-and-place machines are very fast, and on high-frequency performance, because there are no long leads: a 10 mm straight lead adds roughly 7 nanohenries of inductance, while an SMD part has something like one nanohenry, which matters in decoupling and RF.
Through-hole wins on mechanical strength, so you still see it on connectors, switches, large electrolytic capacitors, transformers and heavy inductors, anything that gets plugged, pulled or vibrated.
It's also easier to prototype and rework by hand, and it can handle high power with big leads.

So for a normal modern design I'd go SMT for everything electrical, and through-hole only for parts that take mechanical abuse or carry large current, and I'd try to keep that to one side of the board so only one soldering step is needed."
